OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $f(n)$ be such that, given any $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ with no four points on a circle, there exists some $x_i$ with at least $f(n)$ many distinct distances to other $x_j$. Estimate $f(n)$ - in particular, is it true that\[f(n)>(1-o(1))n?\]Or at least\[f(n) > (1/3+c)n\]for some $c>0$, for all large $n$?
#654: [Er87b,p.168][ErPa90,p.267][Er97e,p.530]
geometry | 
distances
It is trivial that $f(n) \geq (n-1)/3$. In [Er97e] Erdős asks whether $f(n)>(1-o(1))n$, but says this is 'perhaps too optimistic but I am sure that [the trivial bound] can be significantly improved'.
In [Er87b] and [ErPa90] Erdős and Pach ask this under the additional assumption that there are no three points on a line (so that the points are in general position), although they only ask the weaker question whether there is a lower bound of the shape $(\tfrac{1}{3}+c)n$ for some constant $c>0$.
They suggest the lower bound $(1-o(1))n$ is true under the assumption that any circle around a point $x_i$ contains at most $2$ other $x_j$.
The strongest form of this conjecture was disproved by Aletheia [Fe26], which constructed a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no four on a circle, such that there are at most $\frac{3}{4}n$ distinct distances from any single point (although this construction has all the points on the union of two lines, so does not help with the stronger version with the points in general position).

 A few notes on the sources after checking each against the problem statement and DeepMind summary.
The trivial bound, the $(1/3+c)n$ question and the Aletheia bound all check: [Er87b, p. 168] has "Trivially, $d(x_i)\ge (n-1)/3$" and its (3) is $D(n)=\max_i d(x_i) > (1+c)n/3$; [Fe26] Theorem 3 gives $|\mathcal D(u)|<\tfrac34 n$ for every point, with $n=4m$ and the points on the two axes.
One sentence does not match the sources I could read. The page says the $(1-o(1))n$ bound is suggested "under the assumption that any circle around a point $x_i$ contains at most 2 other $x_j$." In [Er87b, p. 168] the weakened hypothesis is "no circle whose center is one of the $x_i$'s goes through more than three of the other $x_i$'s", and it is attached to (3), the $n/3$-scale claim. The at-most-two hypothesis is in Erdős, Some old and new problems in combinatorial geometry (1988), p. 35, question (6): "no four on a circle and every circle whose center is one of the $x_i$ contains at most two of our points. Clearly for every $x_i$ we then have $d(x_i)\ge (n-1)/2$. Is it true that … $\max_i d(x_i) > (1+c),n/2$? I offer 25 dollars for a solution." So "two" goes with $(1+c)n/2$ and "three" with $(1+c)n/3$; neither is paired with $(1-o(1))n$. I have not seen [ErPa90, p. 267] or [Er97e, p. 530], so either may be the source of the page's pairing. 
Two smaller points: [Er87b]'s (4) asks whether a set with $D(n)<(1-c)n$ exists, and [Er87b] is single-authored, so "Erdős and Pach ask" applies to [ErPa90] only.
Disclosure: this literature search was done with AI assistance.
